title: What training is mandatory for employers in Japan?
description: Mandatory employer training in Japan: safety education on hiring and job change, special education, harassment measures, care sector training and licenses.
shortAnswer: As at November 2026, Japan's core mandatory training comes from the Industrial Safety and Health Act, which requires safety and health education when a worker is hired or changes work, special education before designated hazardous work, and licenses or skill training courses for restricted work. Harassment laws require employment management measures, with training as an effort duty. Fixed intervals appear mainly in care sector standards, hospital rules and license renewals.
keyTakeaways: Japanese safety training is triggered by events, not the calendar: education on hiring, on a change of work content, and before designated dangerous or harmful work, backed by criminal penalties.

Japanese law distinguishes binding duties from effort duties. Harassment laws make prevention measures mandatory but phrase training itself as an effort duty, and from October 1, 2026 customer harassment measures are mandatory too.

Annual or twice yearly training is set mostly in care and medical standards: abuse prevention at least once a year in disability and in-home care services, and medical safety training about twice a year in hospitals.

Licensed roles carry renewal courses: hazardous materials handlers within three years of each course, securities sales representatives every five years, and fire prevention managers in larger specified buildings.

Several rules change in 2026 to 2028: harassment law renumbering on October 1, 2026, the amended Whistleblower Protection Act on December 1, 2026, and stress checks for workplaces under 50 workers from April 1, 2028.

sections.heading: How are mandatory training duties set in Japan?

blocks.text: Japanese training duties are set by national acts, detailed in ministerial ordinances and explained in ministry notices and guidelines, and they come in two strengths: binding duties, often backed by fines or criminal penalties, and effort duties that require an employer to endeavor to act. Reading which one applies is the first step for any Japanese training plan, because the same law can make a prevention system mandatory while leaving training as an effort duty.

The Industrial Safety and Health Act is the backbone. It requires safety or health education on hiring and on a change of work content (Article 59(1) and (2)) and special education before workers are assigned to listed dangerous or harmful operations (Article 59(3)) ([Industrial Safety and Health Act](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/347AC0000000057)). The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) sets the details, and Labor Standards Inspection Offices enforce them. The Act sets triggers rather than intervals, which is the opposite of the annual cycle many multinational programs assume; the [refresh cycles guide](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) explains how to combine the two.

Fixed frequencies appear in a different place: interpretive notices for care and medical providers, often enforced through reductions in public fees rather than penalties, and renewal courses for licensed roles administered by prefectures, fire departments and industry bodies. The tables below cover every Japanese regulation page in this library, as at November 2026. Official English translations are not legally binding; only the Japanese texts have legal effect ([Japanese Law Translation](https://www.japaneselawtranslation.go.jp/en)).

sections.heading: What safety and health education must Japanese employers provide?

blocks.text: Every Japanese employer must give safety and health education without delay when a worker is hired or changes work, and special education before designated hazardous work; certain restricted work needs a license or a registered skill training course. Supervisors in listed industries need foreman education, and some workplaces must appoint managers with completed courses.

blocks.text: The penalties show how seriously the event triggers are meant. Breach of Article 59(3) special education is punishable by up to six months of kōkinkei or a fine up to 500,000 yen, and breach of Article 59(1) hiring education by a fine up to 500,000 yen, with corporate fines added by Article 122 ([Industrial Safety and Health Act](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/347AC0000000057)). Foreman education under Article 60 is not listed in either penalty article. The hiring education industry omission was abolished from April 1, 2024, so offices in service industries now owe the full hiring education content.

Coverage is widening. Act No. 33 of 2025 requires sole proprietors and similar persons working at the same site as workers to receive safety and health education for dangerous or harmful work from April 1, 2027, and extends stress checks to workplaces under 50 workers, which MHLW dates to April 1, 2028 ([MHLW](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/11300000/001513749.pdf)). The revised guideline for education of people already in dangerous or harmful work, issued May 25, 2026, also applies from April 1, 2027.

sections.heading: What harassment and workplace conduct training is required?

blocks.text: Japanese employers must take employment management measures against power harassment, sexual harassment and, from October 1, 2026, customer harassment, including a consultation system and a stated policy. Training appears as an effort duty in the acts and as an example method in MHLW guidelines, with training for consultation desk staff listed among the measures.

blocks.text: Article numbers change on October 1, 2026. Act No. 63 of 2025 renumbers the power harassment provisions from Articles 30-2 and 30-3 to Articles 31 and 32, inserts customer harassment as Articles 33 and 34, and moves enforcement to Article 42, which allows advice, guidance, recommendations and publication, with a non criminal fine up to 200,000 yen for failing to report (Article 51) ([Comprehensive Labor Policy Act, from October 1, 2026](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/341AC0000000132/20261001_507AC0000000063)). Course materials and policies that cite Article 30-2 need updating.

The Whistleblower Protection Act amendment raises the stakes from December 1, 2026. It adds an individual penalty of up to six months' imprisonment or a 300,000 yen fine for dismissal or disciplinary action because of a report, a corporate fine up to 30 million yen, a one year presumption of retaliation, and coverage of freelancers ([Consumer Affairs Agency](https://www.caa.go.jp/policies/policy/consumer_partnerships/whisleblower_protection_system/overview/)). The amended commentary adds comprehension tests and videos as example methods, and requires education for designated persons at designation.

sections.heading: What privacy and AI training applies in Japan?

blocks.text: The Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) requires necessary and adequate supervision of employees handling personal data, and the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC) guidelines say businesses must make employees aware of proper handling and give appropriate education. Japan's AI Guidelines for Business expect AI literacy education but are expressly non binding soft law.

blocks.text: The PPC guidelines distinguish 'must' items, which may be judged violations, from 'desirable' items, which are not immediate violations ([PPC guidelines](https://www.ppc.go.jp/personalinfo/legal/guidelines_tsusoku/)). Employee education sits on the 'must' side; risk based frequency sits on the 'desirable' side. An amending act promulgated July 17, 2026 introduces a surcharge and raises penalties, with penalty amendments taking effect six months after promulgation ([PPC](https://www.ppc.go.jp/files/pdf/260717_kaiseihounitsuite.pdf)). For AI, the guidelines are drawn up "through soft laws without any legally binding force", so AI literacy training in Japan is a governance choice rather than a legal duty; see [how to build an AI literacy training program](/guides/how-to-build-an-ai-literacy-training-program).

sections.heading: What anti money laundering training is required in Japan?

blocks.text: The Act on Prevention of Transfer of Criminal Proceeds asks specified business operators to endeavor to provide education and training for employees, and the Financial Services Agency (FSA) guidelines turn human resource development into required actions for the institutions it supervises.

blocks.caption: Anti money laundering training in Japan (as at November 2026)
head: Instrument
Who it covers
Training duty
Frequency
rows: [Act on Prevention of Transfer of Criminal Proceeds, Article 11, and FSA AML/CFT Guidelines](/regulations/japan-fsa-aml-cft-guidelines-training)
Specified business operators; FSA supervised institutions for the Guidelines (except CPAs and audit firms)
Effort duty to provide employee education and training; Guidelines III-5 required actions on human resource development; board involvement; audit of training effectiveness
No fixed interval; update training when national risk assessment or FATF material changes

blocks.text: The legal duty in Article 11 is an effort duty and is outside the Article 18 correction order powers, but supervision gives it weight. The FSA's March 31, 2026 revision kept the III-5 required actions unchanged while deleting the expected action category ([FSA Guidelines](https://www.fsa.go.jp/en/news/2026/20260331/01.pdf)), and the FSA has checked effectiveness verification through inspections since the 2025 program year. Its FAQ says training may include e-learning and must be updated when national risk assessment or FATF material changes, with those already trained verified ([FSA FAQ](https://www.fsa.go.jp/en/news/2026/20260331/02.pdf)). The FATF fifth round on site assessment of Japan is scheduled for June 2028.

blocks.text: Financial sales roles in Japan need a qualification and registration before they can sell, followed by renewal or continuing education run by industry associations. Public school teachers no longer renew licenses but must have their training recorded.

sections.heading: What training do care, medical, pharmaceutical and food employers need?

blocks.text: Care and medical providers in Japan face the country's clearest fixed intervals: abuse prevention, infection control and business continuity training at least once or twice a year under service standards, and medical safety training about twice a year in hospitals. Pharmaceutical and food businesses must train staff and periodically check that training works.

blocks.text: Enforcement in care runs through money. In the fiscal 2024 fee revision, long term care providers that have not implemented elder abuse prevention measures face a 1% fee reduction, and business continuity failures a 3% reduction for facility and residential services ([MHLW](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/12300000/001230329.pdf)); disability welfare providers face a parallel 1% reduction for abuse prevention. The frequencies themselves come from interpretive notices, such as the instruction that abuse prevention training in disability services be held at least once a year and always at hiring ([MHLW](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/001494357.pdf)). A provider's training calendar is therefore also a revenue control.

Hospital rules changed on April 1, 2026, when a medical safety manager role was added who may be directed to deliver staff training, and a 2026 notice set medical safety training at about twice a year with records of date, attendees and topics ([MHLW notice](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/10800000/001685651.pdf)).

sections.heading: What training applies to company drivers in Japan?

blocks.text: Companies that use vehicles above set thresholds must appoint a safe driving manager, who delivers traffic safety education to drivers and runs alcohol checks, and must send the manager to the course run by the Prefectural Public Safety Commission when notified.

blocks.text: Failure to appoint a manager is punishable by a fine up to 500,000 yen, raised from 50,000 yen on October 1, 2022, and detector checks have applied since December 1, 2023 ([National Police Agency](https://www.npa.go.jp/bureau/traffic/insyu/index-2.html)). The NPA's December 2024 circular tells police, on detecting drink driving during work, to investigate employer responsibility, including whether a manager was appointed.

sections.heading: How should an employer in Japan build a single training register?

blocks.text: Build the Japanese register around events and appointments, not annual courses. Most duties fire when something happens to a person (hiring, a change of work, assignment to hazardous work, appointment as a manager) or to the workplace (crossing a headcount threshold, handling a listed substance, entering hot season).

items: **Record the strength of each duty.** Mark each row as binding with a penalty, binding without a penalty (publication, fee reduction), effort duty, or guideline example. This is how Japanese inspectors and counsel read obligations, and it decides where evidence matters most.

**Wire training to HR events.** Hiring and change of work content should automatically create Article 59 education tasks; assignment to any of the 41 special education operations or 16 restricted operations should be blocked until the record exists.

**Track headcount thresholds per workplace.** Managers and committees from 50 workers, promoters from 10, stress checks from 50 until they extend to all workplaces in April 2028, and whistleblowing system duties above 300.
**Track appointment deadlines.** Safety managers, health managers and chemical substance managers are appointed within 14 days; safe driving managers notified within 15 days.
**Record personal renewal dates.** Hazardous materials handler courses, fire prevention manager refreshers, JSDA renewal training and insurance continuing education run on individual cycles.

**Apply the records rules.** Special education records 3 years; committee minutes 3 years; abuse prevention committee records 5 years in disability services; GMP training records 5 years at API sites; alcohol check records 1 year. See [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records each obligation with its source, trigger and strength, so an event such as a job change or an article renumbering identifies the people and learning outcomes affected. Effort duties and guideline expectations can be held separately from binding duties, which keeps the evidence focus where inspectors look. The [knowledge governance](/platform/knowledge-governance) page describes this.

faqs.q: Does Japanese law require annual safety training?
faqs.a: Not as a general rule. The Industrial Safety and Health Act requires education on hiring, on a change of work content and before designated hazardous work, without a periodic interval. Annual or twice yearly training appears in specific standards, such as abuse prevention in care services and medical safety training in hospitals, and in some renewal courses.

faqs.q: Is harassment training mandatory in Japan?
faqs.a: The measures are mandatory: employers must have a policy, a consultation system and response procedures for power harassment and sexual harassment, and from October 1, 2026 for customer harassment. Training itself is phrased as an effort duty in the acts, while the MHLW guidelines list training for staff and consultation desk staff among the measures employers take.

faqs.q: What is an effort duty in Japanese law?
faqs.a: An effort duty requires an employer to endeavor to take a measure rather than guaranteeing it, and it usually carries no direct penalty. Examples include training under Article 32(2) of the Comprehensive Labor Policy Act and employee education under Article 11 of the Act on Prevention of Transfer of Criminal Proceeds. Regulators can still expect evidence of effort.

faqs.q: Do dispatched workers receive training from the agency or the host company?
faqs.a: Both have duties. Under Article 45 of the Worker Dispatch Act, the host is treated as an employer for education on a change of work content and for special education and restricted work, while hiring education is not applied to the host. Article 45(6) prohibits dispatch where the host would breach the special education or restricted work rules.
